html:
A Zen temple in northwest Kyoto, of the Myōshin-ji branch of Rinzai Zen, known for its dry rock garden. The site was an estate of the Fujiwara in the 11th century, and its large pond dates from then. In 1450 the warlord Hosokawa Katsumoto, deputy to the shogun, took the land, built a house there and founded the temple. It was destroyed in the Ōnin War, and his son Hosokawa Masamoto rebuilt it in 1488. Seven emperors of the Heian period are buried in tombs near the temple.

The garden is a dry landscape (karesansui), a rectangle about 25 m by 10 m in front of the abbot's hall. Fifteen stones in five groups, of five, three, three, two and two, sit in white gravel that the monks rake each day; moss around the stones is the only plant. It is meant to be seen sitting on the hall's veranda, and from there at least one stone is always hidden. Behind it runs a low clay wall, stained brown and orange with age. Readings of it range from islands in a stream to tiger cubs crossing water; the garden historian Günter Nitschke held that it stands for nothing and is an abstract composition meant to prompt meditation. Near the tea house a stone water basin bears four characters that, read with its square hole, say "I know only satisfaction".

Who made the garden, and when, is disputed. Most sources place it in the late 15th century, and some credit the painter monk Sōami, but the first clear description, from 1680 to 1682, tells of nine stones, not fifteen. After a fire in 1779 the garden writer Akisato Ritō laid it out again on top of the rubble, and his picture of 1799 shows the garden as it is today. One stone bears the carved names of two kawaramono, low-caste stone workers. The garden inspired a series of works by the composer John Cage, and the temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
